subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Paper 2 Poetry And Prose Texts And Imaginative Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which is the best example of a writer SHOWING rather than TELLING emotion?
options: "She bit her nails and glanced at the door again and again."
questions.explain: Describing actions (nail-biting, glancing) lets the reader infer nervousness, which is "showing."

questions.q: To "zoom in" on the quotation "her hands trembled like leaves in a storm," the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Say it is a nice description
Comment on the simile and what the comparison suggests about her
questions.explain: Zooming in means analysing the chosen technique (a simile) and the specific impression it gives.

questions.q: In a story, a storm rages whenever the hero is angry. The weather reflecting emotion is:
questions.explain: Using weather/nature to mirror a character's mood is pathetic fallacy.

questions.q: "The letter still lay unopened on the mat, its corner curling in the morning sun." What does the detail of the unopened letter most likely IMPLY?
options: The character is keen to read it
Someone is avoiding or dreading its contents
questions.explain: An unopened, neglected letter implies reluctance or dread rather than eagerness.

questions.q: A third-person narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character is described as:
questions.explain: An omniscient narrator has access to all characters' inner thoughts and the wider story.

questions.q: Which is an effective way to vary sentence length for tension in narrative writing?
options: Follow several longer sentences with a short, punchy one: 'He stopped.'
questions.explain: A sudden short sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and tension.

questions.q: You are writing a formal letter to your local council. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: I am writing to express my concern about waste collection in our area.
Hey, listen up about these bins!
Bins are well annoying, sort it out.
So basically the bins are a nightmare.
questions.explain: A formal letter requires a clear, polite statement of purpose in Standard English.

questions.q: An extract begins in the middle of a chase with no introduction of who is running or why. This opening technique is designed to:
options: Explain the whole plot at once
Bore the reader before the action
Plunge the reader straight into the action and create immediacy
questions.explain: Starting mid-action (in medias res) creates immediacy and draws the reader in at once.

questions.q: What is the best way to structure a piece of persuasive writing for impact?
options: Save the main point for a footnote
Put every idea in one giant paragraph
Open with a hook, develop arguments in clear paragraphs, end with a memorable call to action
List random facts in no order
questions.explain: A strong structure hooks, develops logically and ends with a powerful closing message.

questions.q: Which is the most effective, vivid sensory description of a market?
options: There were many people at the market buying food.
Spices stung the air, voices clashed overhead, and ripe mangoes glistened on every stall.
The market was a place where you could buy stuff.
The market was busy and had lots of things.
questions.explain: It engages multiple senses (smell, sound, sight) to create an immersive image.

questions.q: A passage repeatedly uses "net," "tide," "harbour" and "sails." These related words form a:
questions.explain: A group of words linked by topic creates a semantic field, here of the sea.

questions.q: In the persuasive acronym DAFOREST, what does the 'F' stand for?
questions.explain: DAFOREST stands for Direct address, Alliteration, Facts, Opinions, Rhetorical questions, Emotive language, Statistics, Triplets.

questions.q: "The thunder grumbled and the rain drummed on the roof." Which TWO techniques are combined here?
questions.explain: "Grumbled" personifies the thunder while "drummed" imitates sound (onomatopoeia).

questions.q: An exam asks: "How does the writer use language to create a sense of fear?" What should your answer focus on?
options: Specific words and phrases and the effects they create
Retelling the plot of the extract
questions.explain: A "how does the writer use language" question requires analysis of word choices and their effects, not plot summary.

questions.q: "I've told you a million times!" is an example of:
questions.explain: Deliberate exaggeration for effect is hyperbole.

questions.q: A poet uses the same line "and still it rained" at the start of every stanza. This deliberate repetition is best called:
questions.explain: A repeated line used for effect across stanzas is a refrain, a form of repetition.

questions.q: A first-person narrator insists "I did nothing wrong" while describing clearly cruel behaviour. This narrator is best described as:
questions.explain: When the narrator's account conflicts with the evidence, they are an unreliable narrator.

questions.q: Placing "the richest man in the poorest town" side by side to highlight contrast is:
questions.explain: Positioning contrasting ideas together for effect is juxtaposition.

questions.q: A speech opens and closes with the very same phrase, "We will not be moved." Framing a text this way is best described as:
questions.explain: Beginning and ending with the same idea creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: A writer ends a story by returning to the same rainy street where it began. This ending technique is best called:
questions.explain: Returning to the opening situation creates a cyclical (circular) structure.

questions.q: "Time is a thief that steals our youth." This describing of time AS a thief is a:
questions.explain: Calling time a thief directly, without "like" or "as," is a metaphor.

questions.q: A story is told using "I crept down the stairs, my heart pounding." What narrative perspective is this?
questions.explain: The pronoun "I" signals a first-person narrator telling their own experience.
